title: RepoWhisper Analysis
narrative:
# WaveRedact – End‑to‑End Audio Privacy Redaction Toolkit *Automated transcription, sensitive‑entity detection, and audio censoring – all packaged as a single, high‑performance CLI (with an optional HTTP server).* --- ## 1. Introduction Modern organizations increasingly rely on voice recordings – call‑center logs, interview transcripts, meeting minutes – but regulatory frameworks such as **GDPR**, **HIPAA**, and **PCI‑DSS** demand that any personally‑identifiable or regulated information be scrubbed before storage or sharing. **WaveRedact** tackles this problem head‑on. Built around a **Python‑first** code‑base with a **Rust‑backed core** for the most demanding workloads, the project delivers: * **Accurate speech‑to‑text** using OpenAI’s Whisper model. * **Fast rule‑based entity extraction** (regex, GLiNER) complemented by an **LLM‑driven refinement** step when needed. * **Precise audio censoring** – replace sensitive spans with a beep or silence while preserving the surrounding context. * **Compliance‑ready audit reports** that record every redaction, timestamps, and the tool version used. All of this runs locally (or inside a single container), requires no external database, and can be invoked from the command line or via a lightweight HTTP API. The architecture is deliberately **modular** and **extensible**, allowing teams to swap models, add new privacy rules, or integrate WaveRedact into larger pipelines with minimal friction. --- ## 2. Architectural Overview | Layer | Primary Responsibility | Key Modules | |------|------------------------|-------------| | **Entry point** | CLI parsing, configuration, orchestration kickoff | `cli/main.py` | | **Application orchestrator** | Coordinates GPU setup, transcription, extraction, censoring, reporting | `app.py` | | **Core services** | Low‑level GPU handling, memory cleanup, compliance reporting, optional Llama server | `core/gpu_setup.py`, `core/memory_manager.py`, `services/compliance.py`, `services/llama_server.py` | | **Factories** | Uniform creation of heavyweight models (Whisper, GLiNER) | `factories/whisper_factory.py`, `factories/gliner_factory.py`, `factories/factory.py` | | **Pipeline** | Chunking, mapping, extraction (regex, GLiNER, LLM), orchestration of the privacy‑pipeline | `pipeline/chunk.py`, `pipeline/mapper.py`, `pipeline/extractors/*`, `pipeline/privacy_pipeline.py`, `pipeline/orchestrator.py` | | **Audio I/O** | Discover, load, and write audio files; apply masks (beep / silence) | `audio/audio_manager.py`, `audio/audio_censor.py` | | **Transcription** | Whisper‑driven speech‑to‑text with word‑level timestamps | `services/transcribe.py` | | **Utilities** | Console styling, path resolution, level selection, shared constants | `utils/console.py`, `utils/path_utils.py`, `config/level.py` | | **Rust extension** | GPU‑accelerated helpers, low‑level memory management (exposed via `pyo3`) | `waveredact_core/` (compiled to `waveredact_core.pyi`) | ### 2.1 Design Patterns * **Clean / Hexagonal Architecture** – each layer communicates through well‑defined interfaces, keeping business logic independent of I/O, UI, or external services. * **Factory Method** – model creation (`WhisperFactory`, `GlinerFactory`) is encapsulated, making it trivial to switch to a different model family or a custom checkpoint. * **Strategy (Extractor)** – the pipeline can combine any number of extractors that implement the same abstract contract (`BaseExtractor`). * **Orchestrator / Pipeline** – a lightweight data‑flow engine that processes overlapping text chunks, merges results, and optionally invokes an LLM for ambiguous cases. ### 2.2 Runtime Stack | Component | Typical Library (inferred) | |-----------|----------------------------| | **Python** | `click` (CLI), `rich` (styled console), `pydantic`/`dataclasses`, `torch`, `transformers`, `whisper`, `gliner`, `pydub` (audio), `requests` (LLM server) | | **Rust** | `pyo3` + `maturin` for the compiled extension (`waveredact_core`) | | **HTTP Server (optional)** | Likely **FastAPI** or **Flask** (lightweight) – wrapped by `services/llama_server.py` | | **Packaging** | `uv` for dependency lockfiles, `PyInstaller` (`waveredact.spec`) for a single‑binary distribution | | **CI/CD** | GitHub Actions (`pytest.yaml`, `release.yaml`) | --- ## 3. Module Walk‑through Below each major package is described in logical order, showing how the pieces interlock to achieve the end‑to‑end workflow. ### 3.1 Utilities | Module | Purpose | Highlights | |--------|---------|------------| | **`utils/console.py`** | Central `rich.Console` with a colour theme (`info`, `warning`, `error`, `success`). | Guarantees uniform, readable terminal output across the whole project. | | **`utils/path_utils.py`** | Resolves the project root (including PyInstaller “frozen” mode) and a persistent per‑OS data directory. | Enables safe storage of downloaded models, caches, and server binaries. | | **`config/level.py`** | Defines privacy‑censoring tiers (`base`, `medium`, `total`) and a `LevelSetter` that validates custom label JSON files. | Guarantees that only supported entity labels are ever passed to extractors. | ### 3.2 Core Services | Module | Responsibility | Key Behaviour | |--------|----------------|---------------| | **`core/gpu_setup.py`** | Detects CUDA availability, downloads missing NVIDIA DLLs on Windows, injects them into the process. | Returns the optimal device string (`cuda`, `mps`, `cpu`) and compute type (`int8_float16` vs `int8`). | | **`core/memory_manager.py`** | Proactively frees Python GC and GPU caches; reports free RAM in GB. | Allows the pipeline to adapt batch sizes based on current system memory. | | **`services/compliance.py`** | Generates a JSON audit report containing filenames, timestamps, redaction details, and WaveRedact version. | Provides the evidence required for regulatory audits. | | **`services/llama_server.py`** | Downloads a platform‑specific Llama server binary, launches it, monitors health, and tears it down cleanly. | Supplies a local LLM endpoint for the optional refinement step. | | **`services/transcribe.py`** | Wraps a Whisper model to produce word‑level timestamps and a mapping from sequential indices → words / interval strings. | Supplies the textual backbone for all downstream extraction. | ### 3.3 Factories (Model Builders) | Module | What it builds | Extensibility | |--------|----------------|---------------| | **`factories/factory.py`** | Abstract base `Factory` with a `build()` contract. | Guarantees a consistent API for any future factory (e.g., a new ASR model). | | **`factories/whisper_factory.py`** | Constructs a Whisper model, automatically selecting the correct device & compute type via `GPUEnvironmentManager`. | Swap Whisper versions (`tiny`, `base`, `large`) simply by changing the model identifier. | | **`factories/gliner_factory.py`** | Downloads, sanitises, and loads a GLiNER2 privacy‑filter model. | Adding a new GLiNER checkpoint or custom entity set only requires a different model ID. | ### 3.4 Audio Management | Module | Core Functions | |--------|----------------| | **`audio/audio_manager.py`** | • Normalises input paths (single file vs directory).
• Discovers supported audio files (`.mp3`, `.wav`, `.flac`, `.m4a`, `.ogg`).
• Saves censored audio, falling back to alternate codecs when required. | | **`audio/audio_censor.py`** | • Accepts a list of interval strings (start‑end seconds) and a mask type (`beep` or `silence`).
• Delegates the heavy‑lifting to the Rust extension `censor_audio`.
• Writes the censored file to a sibling `censored/` folder (or a custom output directory). | ### 3.5 Extraction Pipeline | Module | Role in the pipeline | |--------|----------------------| | **`pipeline/chunk.py`** | Splits the transcription (index → word) into overlapping chunks (`batch_size`, `overlap`). Keeps context across chunk boundaries for better LLM performance. | | **`pipeline/mapper.py`** | Maps a chunk’s concatenated string back to the original word indices, enabling precise timestamp retrieval for any character span. | | **`pipeline/extractors/base_extractor.py`** | Abstract contract – each extractor returns `(start, end, confidence, label)`. | | **`pipeline/extractors/regex_extractor.py`** | Fast, deterministic detection of common PII (emails, credit‑card numbers, IPs, dates, etc.) using pre‑compiled regexes. | | **`pipeline/extractors/gliner_extractor.py`** | Calls the GLiNER2 model to locate entity spans for the configured label set, returning sorted, de‑duplicated results. | | **`pipeline/models/model.py`** | Abstract LLM model interface – `run_model` receives a text chunk and ambiguous indices, returns a dict `{idx: label}`. | | **`pipeline/models/gguf.py`** | Concrete implementation for locally‑hosted GGUF LLMs (e.g., Llama). Handles prompt construction, JSON response parsing, and hallucination healing. | | **`pipeline/privacy_pipeline.py`** | Orchestrates **rule‑based** (`RegexExtractor`, `GlinerExtractor`) and **LLM‑based** (`GGUFModel`) extraction. Produces two structures:
• `labels_by_idx` – final mapping of word indices → entity label.
• `locked_idxs` – high‑confidence indices that are automatically redacted. | | **`pipeline/orchestrator.py`** | Drives the end‑to‑end flow for each audio chunk:
1. Run `DataPrivacyPipeline` (fast extractors).
2. Optionally ask the user to approve results (interactive mode).
3. If needed, invoke the LLM refinement step (`run_llm_extraction`).
4. Aggregate final labels for the whole file. | ### 3.6 Application Layer | Module | Summary | |--------|---------| | **`app.py`** | The **WaveRedactApplication** glues everything together:
• Prepares the GPU environment.
• Instantiates Whisper and GLiNER via factories.
• Determines the privacy level (or custom label file).
• Builds the extraction pipeline and orchestrator.
• Calls `AudioCensor` with the final timestamps.
• Generates the compliance report and shuts down any Llama server. | | **`cli/main.py`** | Click‑based command line interface. Exposes options for:
• Input (`--file` / `--folder`).
• Redaction level (`--level`).
• Automatic mode (`--auto`).
• LLM usage (`--use-llm`).
• Censor mask (`--censor-mode`).
Provides an interactive approval callback that displays detected words before committing to censoring. | --- ## 4. End‑to‑End Workflow (What Happens When You Run the CLI) 1. **Startup** – CLI parses arguments, creates an `AppConfig`, and launches `WaveRedactApplication`. 2. **GPU & Environment** – `GPUEnvironmentManager` ensures CUDA (or Apple MPS) is ready; `MemoryManager` reports free RAM. 3. **Model Loading** – * Whisper model via `WhisperFactory`. * GLiNER2 model via `GlinerFactory`. * (Optionally) a local GGUF LLM via `LLamaServer` + `GGUFModel`. 4. **Audio Discovery** – `IOAudioManager.get_audio()` yields a list of supported audio files. 5. **Transcription** – `TranscribeService` produces word‑level timestamps (`idx → word` & `idx → interval`). 6. **Chunking** – `Chunker` slices the transcription into overlapping windows. 7. **Extraction** – For each chunk: * `DataPrivacyPipeline` runs regex + GLiNER extractors, maps character spans back to word indices (`ChunkMapper`). * High‑confidence detections are *locked*; ambiguous indices are collected. * If LLM refinement is enabled (or the user requests it), `GGUFModel` processes the ambiguous indices and the results are merged. 8. **Censoring** – All locked intervals are passed to `AudioCensor`, which calls the Rust `censor_audio` routine to replace the audio with either a beep or silence. The censored file is saved alongside the original. 9. **Compliance Reporting** – `ComplianceManager.generate_report()` writes a JSON audit file summarising: original & censored filenames, timestamps, detected words, and the privacy level used. 10. **Shutdown** – Any spawned Llama server is terminated; the CLI prints a friendly closing message. --- ## 5. Extending WaveRedact | Area | How to extend | Example | |------|---------------|---------| | **New ASR model** | Implement a new factory subclass (e.g., `MyASRFactory

raw_modules.explanation: The file creates a reusable Rich console instance for formatted terminal output. It first defines a theme mapping logical message categories—info, warning, error, and success—to specific color styles. Using that theme, it constructs a `Console` object that applies these styles automatically when printing. The resulting `console` can be imported elsewhere to emit consistently colored messages without redefining styling each time. This centralizes UI appearance and simplifies colored logging throughout the project.

The IOAudioManager class centralizes handling of audio files within a given directory or single file path. Upon instantiation it normalizes the input path, ensures the target directory exists (when not a single file), and records whether it should treat the path as a file. get_audio() scans the resolved location, filters for supported extensions (mp3, wav, flac, m4a, ogg), and returns a list of Path objects for valid audio files, issuing console warnings for unsupported types. save_censored() receives a processed AudioSegment, builds a new filename by appending “_censored” before the original extension, and attempts to export the audio in its original format. If the export fails due to missing codecs (e.g., OGG without libvorbis) it falls back to an alternative codec or to WAV, printing appropriate console messages. Finally, the method confirms the saved location and returns the full output path.

The module defines an `AudioMaskTypes` enum to choose between a beep or silence mask.  
`AudioCensor` is initialized with an audio manager, a mapping of interval strings, a list of indices to censor, and an optional relative output directory; it creates the output folder if needed.  
It extracts the start‑end times for the selected indices, converts them to floats, and stores them as intervals.  
When `censor_file` is called, the input audio is loaded, its sample width normalized, and each interval is expanded slightly to avoid cutting too close to speech boundaries.  
The raw audio bytes together with format metadata and the padded intervals are handed to the core `censor_audio` routine, which returns modified byte data according to the chosen mask type.  
The method rebuilds an `AudioSegment` from the censored bytes, determines a destination folder (either the provided one or a “censored” subfolder next to the source), and uses the audio manager to write the censored file, returning its path.

The file defines a `Levels` enumeration that groups privacy‑censoring labels into three tiers: base, medium, and total, each tier expanding on the previous one.  
`LevelSetter` orchestrates how a user selects one of these tiers, either by reading a command‑line flag, prompting interactively with a menu, or loading a custom JSON label list.  
When a custom label file is supplied, the setter forces the total tier and validates the file’s existence, JSON syntax, list structure, and that every label is supported by the predefined sets.  
The validation process converts both the user‑provided and full label collections to sets, computes any unsupported entries, and raises informative errors if mismatches occur.  
Finally, the chosen tier’s label collection is stored in `target_labels` for downstream redaction logic.

The module provides two utility functions for locating filesystem paths used by the application. `get_project_root` determines the project’s base directory, returning the temporary PyInstaller extraction folder when the program is frozen, otherwise the source tree’s root. `get_app_data_dir` computes a persistent data directory appropriate to the current operating system—using the Windows %APPDATA% location, macOS Library/Application Support, or a hidden folder in the user’s home on Linux/Unix. It then guarantees that this directory exists by creating any missing parent folders. These helpers centralize path resolution, enabling the rest of the code to store models, servers, and other resources reliably across platforms.

The file defines a GPUEnvironmentManager that detects whether a CUDA‑capable GPU is available and records the appropriate device string. When running on Windows with CUDA selected, it guarantees the required NVIDIA DLLs are present by creating a folder, downloading a zip of the libraries, extracting the needed files, and then adding that directory to the process DLL search path. If the DLLs are already present, it skips the download step and proceeds directly to injection. The manager also prints the detected hardware and logs successful injection, while handling any injection errors with a warning. Finally, it exposes helper methods to return the best compute type for the detected device (int8_float16 for CUDA, int8 for CPU).

The file defines a MemoryManager class that centralizes runtime memory housekeeping. Its clean_memory method forces Python’s garbage collector to run and then clears any GPU‑related caches, supporting Apple MPS devices when available and CUDA GPUs otherwise. The get_available_ram method queries the operating system for free physical memory, converting the value to gigabytes for easy consumption. If the system query fails, it returns a safe default of 8 GB. This utility enables programs that use PyTorch to free resources proactively and to adapt behavior based on current RAM availability.

The file defines an abstract base class that serves as a generic factory contract for creating objects. It inherits from the standard abstract‑base‑class infrastructure, ensuring that subclasses must implement the required behavior. The sole abstract method, `build`, is declared to return an unrestricted type, allowing any concrete product to be produced. By marking the method with an ellipsis placeholder, the class signals that concrete implementations will provide the actual creation logic. This design enables a consistent, interchangeable interface for constructing diverse model instances across the codebase.

The file defines a GlinerFactory class that extends a generic Factory to manage the GLiNER2 privacy‑filter model. Its constructor stores the desired model ID, confidence threshold, a safe cache directory under the application data folder, and the list of entity labels to extract. The build() method checks whether the model files already exist; if not, it creates the cache directory and downloads the model snapshot from Hugging Face, informing the user of progress. It then sanitizes the downloaded tokenizer_config.json by removing any extra_special_tokens field that can cause loading errors, handling failures with a logged warning and termination. Finally, the method silently loads the model from the local cache using GLiNER2.from_pretrained and returns the ready‑to‑use instance.

The file defines a `WhisperFactory` that implements a generic `Factory` interface for creating Whisper speech‑to‑text models. It stores the desired model identifier and a `GPUEnvironmentManager` used to configure hardware resources. When `build()` is called, it asks the GPU manager for the appropriate device and compute type, then constructs a `WhisperModel` with those settings. The resulting model is ready for inference on the selected hardware. This encapsulates model instantiation logic, keeping GPU configuration separate from the rest of the application.

The file defines an abstract base class that standardizes how language‑model extractors are implemented. It mandates a single method, `run_model`, which processes a text chunk represented as a mapping from positions to words. The method also receives an optional list of indices that were ambiguous for a preceding extractor. Implementations must return a dictionary that maps each identified sensitive position to its corresponding entity label. This contract ensures interchangeable model components within the extraction pipeline.

The file defines **GGUFModel**, a concrete implementation of the generic Model interface for locally‑hosted GGUF language models.  
During initialization it determines the model storage path, loads system and user prompts from a YAML file, ensures the model file is present (downloading it from HuggingFace if missing), and creates an OpenAI‑compatible client that talks to the local inference server.  
A `labels` property lets callers set the list of sensitive categories the model should look for.  
When `run_model` is called, it formats the supplied text chunk and optional ambiguous indices into the user prompt, sends the request to the local LLM, and expects a JSON‑formatted response.  
The private `_parse_llm_response` method extracts the JSON object from the raw text, falling back to regex‑based reconstruction if parsing fails.  
`_extract_ids_with_healing` examines the parsed “word_analysis” array, validates reported IDs against the original chunk, and attempts to recover mismatched (hallucinated) IDs by searching for the reported word.  
Finally, `run_model` returns a dictionary mapping each confirmed sensitive word’s ID to its label, or an empty dict on failure.

The file defines a Chunker class that partitions a sequence of indexed words into overlapping segments. Its constructor validates that the overlap size is smaller than the maximum segment length and stores both parameters. The chunk_text method converts the input mapping of indices‑to‑tokens into an ordered list, then walks through it with a step equal to batch_size minus overlap, extracting slices of up to batch_size items each. Each slice is turned back into a dictionary representing a chunk, and the process stops once the final slice reaches the end of the data. The result is a list of these overlapping chunk dictionaries, suitable for downstream processing that requires context continuity across boundaries.

The file defines an abstract base class that serves as a common contract for all sensitive‑data extraction components. It mandates that any concrete extractor implement a single method responsible for scanning a text segment and locating sensitive entities. The method must return a collection of records, each containing the start and end character offsets, a confidence score, and a label identifying the entity type. By using the abstract base class, the system can treat different extractors uniformly while ensuring they all provide the required output format. This design enables interchangeable, plug‑in style implementations for various data‑privacy use cases.

The file defines a GlinerExtractor class that inherits from a generic extractor base. It stores a GLiNER2 model together with a list of target entity labels and a confidence threshold. When extract is called with a text string, it asks the model to return entities matching the target labels, including their character spans and confidence scores. It then iterates over the model’s output, normalizing each entity into a tuple of start offset, end offset, confidence, and label, while deduplicating via a set. Finally, it returns these tuples sorted by their start position, providing a clean, ordered list of detected sensitive entities.

The file defines a `RegexExtractor` that inherits from a generic extractor base. During initialization it receives an optional list of target labels and builds a collection of compiled regular‑expression patterns only for those labels, mapping each pattern to its original label. The supported labels include common sensitive data types such as email, IBAN, credit‑card numbers, phone numbers, IP addresses, tax IDs, national IDs, and dates, each expressed with a robust pattern that tolerates variations (e.g., “dot”, “punto”, or different separators). The `extract` method iterates over every stored pattern, finds all matches in the supplied text, and records each match’s start and end offsets, a fixed confidence score of 1.0, and the associated label. The result is a list of tuples suitable for downstream processing or redaction.

ChunkMapper receives a dictionary that links original word indices to their textual content. It concatenates the words in order, constructing a single string while recording each word’s start‑and‑end character offsets in a mapping. The internal mapping lets the class translate any character span back to the set of original indices whose words intersect that span. The `get_original_idxs` method iterates over the stored offsets, selecting indices whose ranges overlap the supplied start and end positions. This enables downstream code to locate the original transcription positions that correspond to arbitrary substrings of the combined chunk.

The DataPrivacyPipeline coordinates two kinds of extractors: lightweight BaseExtractor instances that work without a language model, and optional LLM‑based Model extractors. Its extract_sensitive_data method runs each simple extractor over the original text, translates the character spans returned into original word indices via a ChunkMapper, records the associated label for every index, and automatically “locks” any index whose confidence exceeds a configurable threshold. The method returns a dictionary of all detected indices mapped to their labels together with the set of locked indices that must be redacted. When some indices remain ambiguous, extract_sensitive_with_llm feeds those indices and the original chunk to each LLM extractor, merges the resulting index‑label pairs, and returns the refined mapping. Thus the pipeline first performs fast rule‑based detection, then refines uncertain cases with a language model, producing a complete label map and a list of high‑confidence redactions.

The **Orchestrator** coordinates the privacy‑redaction workflow by feeding each audio chunk into a `DataPrivacyPipeline` and aggregating the resulting entity labels. It iterates over all `ChunkMapper` objects, collecting confident detections, tracking ambiguous indices, and optionally reporting progress through a callback. When interactive mode is enabled, it asks the user (or a supplied approval callback) whether to accept the initial results; a negative answer triggers an LLM‑based refinement if configured. In non‑interactive runs, the presence of the `--use-llm` flag determines whether the LLM step is invoked automatically for higher precision. The `run_llm_extraction` method processes each chunk’s ambiguous indices with the pipeline’s LLM extractor, merges the LLM‑validated labels with previously locked high‑confidence labels, and returns the final index‑to‑entity mapping. This mapping represents all words that should be censored according to the combined regex, GLiNER, and optional LLM analyses.

The file defines a ComplianceManager that produces JSON audit reports for a privacy‑redaction pipeline. Its generate_report method receives a collection of redaction results and, if the list is empty, exits without action. For a single result it records the original and censored filenames directly; for multiple results it aggregates those fields into lists, while always attaching a UTC timestamp and the software version. The redaction details from each result are collected under a redactions key, preserving the original structure of the objects. Finally, the assembled report dictionary is serialized to the specified path with pretty‑printed JSON.

The file defines a service that automatically obtains the appropriate Llama model server binary for the host OS, downloads and extracts it if missing, and ensures it is executable. It determines the latest compatible release via the GitHub API, falling back to a known version when the request fails. When started, it checks that the configured port is free, computes optimal GPU layer settings based on system memory or NVIDIA‑GPU free VRAM, and launches the server in a subprocess with sensible thread counts. It then polls the server’s health endpoint until the service reports readiness, raising an error if the server does not start in time. The class also provides a method to terminate the subprocess cleanly, and registers this cleanup to run on interpreter exit. Throughout, informative console messages keep the user apprised of progress and any warnings.

The file defines a TranscribeService class that wraps a WhisperModel instance to perform speech‑to‑text conversion. Its constructor stores the model and initializes an empty string to accumulate the full transcription. transcribe_audio receives a file path, runs the model’s transcribe method with word‑level timestamps, and iterates over the returned segments, appending each word to full_text while building parallel lists of raw words and their “start‑end” interval strings. After processing all segments, the method returns two dictionaries: one mapping sequential indices to the collected words, and another mapping the same indices to the corresponding interval strings. The private helper _compute_idx_pair creates these index‑to‑string mappings by enumerating the supplied list.

The WaveRedactApplication coordinates audio redaction by first ensuring the GPU environment is ready and loading a Whisper transcription model (or using a supplied one). It transcribes each input file (or all files in a folder) into word‑level timestamps, then selects an LLM model based on available RAM and optionally starts a local Llama server. Label definitions are built from the chosen privacy level (or custom file), after which a GLiNER extractor and a regex extractor are instantiated and combined with the LLM extractor into a privacy‑pipeline. Audio text is split into manageable chunks, each chunk is processed by an orchestrator that applies the extractors, optionally asks the user for approval, and aggregates the identified sensitive indices. The resulting timestamps are fed to an AudioCensor which either beeps or silences the intervals, and adjacent redactions of the same type are merged into concise ranges. Finally, a compliance report summarizing filenames, censored paths, detected words, and redaction intervals is written, and any running LLM server is cleanly stopped.

The script initializes environment variables and configures logging, then defines a callback that displays detected sensitive words and asks the user to confirm their correctness.  
A Click‑based command‑line interface accepts options for redaction level, automatic mode, LLM usage, censor mode, a target file or folder, and an optional custom‑labels file.  
It validates that exactly one of --file or --folder is supplied, constructs an AppConfig object from the parsed arguments, and injects the approval callback.  
A WaveRedactApplication instance is created with this configuration and executed, performing the audio redaction workflow.  
Finally, the program prints a closing message, and the entry point ensures multiprocessing compatibility before invoking the CLI.
